The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on near-term economic activity and pose clear downside risks to the outlook, but the FOMC’s emergency move to a 0–0.25 percent target range, large-scale Treasury and agency MBS purchases, and expanded repo and discount-window support are aligned with the literature on how accommodative policy can cushion demand and credit shocks. Credit-channel research (Bernanke–Gertler; Oliner and Rudebusch; Gertler–Gilchrist) finds that easing and liquidity backstops compress external finance premia and are especially supportive for bank-dependent and smaller firms; swap lines further stabilize dollar funding conditions. With market-based inflation compensation falling and inflation below 2 percent, models that highlight deflation and liquidity-trap risks argue for front-loaded easing and expectations management; inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson) helps anchor expectations around the symmetric 2 percent goal. Net assessment: near-term growth is negatively affected, but decisive policy materially reduces macro-financial tail risks relative to inaction.
